say.text: Worked example. A child with known TOF. I will reason aloud; you watch.
Step 1, **ECG**. It shows right axis deviation, prominent R or qR waves in V1 and upright T waves in V1.
Read together: right atrial enlargement and **right ventricular hypertrophy**. The right side is the loaded side.

choices.label: Why is it the right ventricle?

say.text: The fourth component of classic TOF is right ventricular hypertrophy, so an ECG that reads RVH fits.
It is **not** left ventricular hypertrophy, whatever an old option list tells you.
Step 2, **chest X-ray**. Same child, same logic. StatPearls describes a normal-size heart silhouette with an upturned apex and a concave main pulmonary artery segment.
The upturned apex is attributed to RVH. So **boot-shaped** describes the shape, not an enlarged heart.

choices.label: Go deeper: do all infants show it?

say.text: Most infants with TOF, however, may not show the boot-shaped finding.
Your turn to explain my step 2. On the boot-shaped film, what does the **upturned apex** reflect?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Which ventricle is the fourth component of TOF? Think of the one that works against the obstruction.
Try again.
Yes. The upturned apex is attributed to right ventricular hypertrophy, with a concave pulmonary arterial segment.
Tempting, because LVH is the ventricle everyone learns first and old option lists include it. But it is the right ventricle: RVH is one of the four components, and PYQs keyed LVH as not part of TOF.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so pause here: the apex and the ECG both point to the right ventricle.

say.text: Tempting, because a boot sounds big. But StatPearls describes a normal-size heart silhouette with an upturned apex.
The apex is upturned by RVH, not stretched by a big heart.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so remember: boot-shaped is about shape, not size.

say.text: Another child with TOF has a film with a **normal-size** heart, an upturned apex and a concave pulmonary segment.
What best describes it?
A normal-size silhouette is not cardiomegaly, and the upturned apex is attributed to right ventricular hypertrophy.
Step 3, **confirm**. The echocardiogram is the gold standard for diagnosis and remains the primary diagnostic modality.
It shows the abnormal anatomy directly. ECG and X-ray only suggest.
Adjuncts: contrast-enhanced **CT** shows the complex morphology; **MRI** gives anatomy and function without ionising radiation.
Echocardiography has limitations in assessing extracardiac anomalies such as peripheral pulmonary stenosis and atresia.
CT can evaluate post-surgical changes, such as patency of palliative shunts.
Pulmonary artery assessment matters: repairing the cardiac defects without addressing pulmonary artery hypoplasia or stenosis has a poor outcome.
The main or right pulmonary artery diameter should be compared with that of the ascending aorta.

Tempting, because the boot and the RVH are the classic signs and you just read them. But a classic sign is not the gold standard: echocardiography is.

say.text: A table asks: gold standard investigation for diagnosis of TOF. Which?
The boot is a classic X-ray sign, but the gold standard for diagnosis is the echocardiogram.

What does it indicate?
Yes: right atrial enlargement and right ventricular hypertrophy.
Tempting, because LVH is the usual ECG pattern you meet. But right axis deviation with tall R in V1 is right-sided: right atrial enlargement and RVH.

ECG shows RVH but does not confirm the anatomy. The echocardiogram is the gold standard.
Last piece. Echo is done and the surgeon wants an adjunct giving anatomy **and** function without ionising radiation. Which?
Yes. MRI provides anatomical detail and functional information without ionising radiation.
CT is the other adjunct, useful for complex morphology.
Close: contrast-enhanced CT is a useful adjunct for complex morphology. But the one described as giving anatomy and function without ionising radiation is MRI.
A chest X-ray is not an adjunct imaging step; the diagnosis rests on echo, with CT and MRI as adjuncts.
